title: Speed camera penalties and community safety zones
subtitle: Committee also heard long-term financial sustainability update, delegations on safety for older adults and children, and a closed session on land.
overview: The Administration and Finance Committee recommended that Regional Council enact the bylaws and policy for an Administrative Penalty Program covering camera-based speed enforcement {{vote:m3}}. Under the program, a ticket can be appealed first to a regional screening officer and then to an independent hearing officer. The committee also recommended adopting a two-step warrant for choosing Community Safety Zones on regional roads {{vote:m4}}. Fines for speeding double in those zones, and staff will report back on school zones and other candidate areas.

A motion to end debate on the penalty program was defeated {{vote:m2}} after some members objected that colleagues had not yet spoken. Staff said the program can be scaled up gradually, with about 32 cameras added each year toward 175 by 2028, and the 2025 locations are being proposed by area municipalities. Staff also proposed moving the program start from November to early January.

The committee received a long-term financial sustainability report for information ahead of the 2025 budget, and approved the consent agenda {{vote:m1}}. After the meeting it went into closed session on a proposed land acquisition. The minutes report no decision from that session.

decisions.item: Administrative Penalty Program for speed cameras
decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council enact the Administrative Penalty Program Bylaw and the Hearing Officer Bylaw, and approve the Appointment and Conduct of Hearing Officers Policy {{vote:m3}}.
The committee recommended adopting the Two-Step Community Safety Zone Warrant as the preferred method for identifying zones on regional roads {{vote:m4}}.

decisions.item: Community Safety Zones at camera school zones
decisions.detail: The same recommendation adopts a strategy of designating a Community Safety Zone at every regional-road school zone that will get a speed camera.
Staff are directed to report back on school zones needing the designation before the late-2024 camera changes, and to list other prospective zones with staffing and resource impacts.
The committee received the consent agenda items for information and approved them {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Supporters said speeding is among the most common complaints from residents. They described the cameras as a way to change driver behaviour that police cannot provide everywhere, and said a ticket can be avoided by not speeding. One councillor said safety, not revenue, is the purpose.

Opponents and sceptics said the business case, based on 175 cameras, 5,000 tickets per camera and a $60 average fine, was too ambitious. One councillor called it a cash grab and said the doubling of fines through the penalty program was not stated clearly in earlier reports. Staff said it appeared in the business case but not explicitly in a report.

Some members raised the cost of fines for households with little savings, and the 24-hour operation of cameras. A delegate and one councillor noted that other behaviours, such as U-turns, three-point turns and distracted driving, may pose more risk near schools than speeding. Staff said consistent, all-hours rules avoid confusion.

Some councillors said area municipal councils were not directly consulted, since the work was done staff to staff. Others said the issue has been discussed since 2020 and that local staff should brief their own councils. Several members objected to the name 'municipal speed cameras' because complaints may go to local municipalities. Staff said cameras on municipal roads need that road authority's support.

Delegates asked that Community Safety Zones extend beyond school zones, which are defined by where a school driveway meets the road, to cover older adult residences, community centres and busy school routes. They also asked for longer crossing times and public education. In the finance discussion, one councillor questioned the reserves, which are low compared with other regions. Staff said the debt-to-reserve ratio is improving.
